title: Establishment of an ex vivo vascular tissue model to investigate bunyavirus-triggered vascular endothelial injury.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome, an emerging infectious disease caused by the tick-borne bunyavirus severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV), is associated with a high clinical fatality rate of 12%-50%. The mechanisms underlying virus-induced vascular injury remain poorly defined due to the lack of physiologically relevant human tissue models.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study established an ex vivo human vascular tissue model to investigate bunyavirus-triggered vascular endothelial injury. The model supports productive bunyavirus infection and enables quantitative assessment of endothelial injury, tissue damage, and antiviral efficacy.
analysis.methods: The ex vivo human vascular tissue model was used to study bunyavirus infection, with viral nucleoprotein detection and viral amplification serving as evidence of successful infection. Histopathological analysis, TUNEL staining, and transcriptional changes were employed to assess endothelial injury and tissue damage.
analysis.main_results: Histopathological analysis, TUNEL staining, and endothelial injury-associated transcriptional changes revealed irregular venous tissue structure, luminal endothelial disruption, and apoptosis following infection. Both SFTSV and Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV) can successfully infect ex vivo human vascular tissue.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate that bunyavirus infection triggers endothelial disruption and that antiviral compounds can suppress viral replication and alleviate infection-associated tissue injury. This model provides a valuable experimental system for studying virus-vascular interactions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This model enables evaluation of antiviral compound efficacy, demonstrating that niclosamide or 4'-fluorouridine significantly inhibits SFTSV and RVFV replication in ex vivo vascular tissues. These findings establish the ex vivo human vascular tissue as a valuable tool for investigating bunyavirus-induced vascular pathogenesis.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report specific limitations of the study design. The evidence strength is high as the findings are based on direct observations and experimental validation using ex vivo human vascular tissue.

analysis.summary_en: This study establishes an ex vivo human vascular tissue model to investigate bunyavirus-triggered vascular endothelial injury, specifically focusing on severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV). The model demonstrates that SFTSV and Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV) can infect vascular tissue, leading to endothelial disruption and apoptosis. Histopathological analysis, TUNEL staining, and transcriptional changes reveal these effects, while antiviral compounds like niclosamide or 4'-fluorouridine significantly inhibit viral replication. The model provides a valuable tool for studying vascular pathogenesis and evaluating antiviral therapeutics against emerging bunyaviruses. The findings highlight the importance of developing physiologically relevant models to understand and combat vascular injuries caused by bunyaviruses, with high confidence due to direct experimental evidence.

title: A highly potent bispecific antibody confers complete protection against SFTSV in preclinical models.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) is an emerging bunyavirus that causes severe human disease, with a case fatality rate of up to 30%. However, no licensed therapeutics are currently available for clinical use.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study identified two SFTSV neutralizing nanobodies (Nbs), N2C1 and N2D2, which were tested in preclinical models.
analysis.methods: Structural analysis revealed that N2C1 spanned Gn domain I and domain III, while N2D2 targeted domain I, located at the inner and outer sides of the Gn-Gc hexamer crown, respectively. They also exhibited synergistic neutralization, and their bispecific antibody (bsAb) displayed dramatically enhanced neutralizing potency.
analysis.main_results: In a lethal mouse model, the bsAb demonstrated superior protective efficacy over the parental Nbs in both preexposure and postexposure administration regimens. In preclinical ferret models, the bsAb N2D2-Fc-N2C1 conferred complete protection against SFTSV not only at a low dose of 5 mg/kg but also when administered as late as 2 d postinfection.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The bsAb N2D2-Fc-N2C1 demonstrated potent protective efficacy, supporting its development as a promising clinical candidate against SFTSV infection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The bsAb N2D2-Fc-N2C1 can confer complete protection against SFTSV in preclinical models, which could inform future studies and clinical applications for SFTSV infection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: More studies are needed to confirm the efficacy and safety of the bsAb in human clinical trials. The study is limited by the use of preclinical models, which may not fully represent human disease.

analysis.summary_en: This study identified and characterized two SFTSV neutralizing nanobodies, N2C1 and N2D2, which were combined into a bispecific antibody (bsAb) that demonstrated superior protective efficacy in preclinical models. The bsAb N2D2-Fc-N2C1 conferred complete protection against SFTSV, supporting its potential as a promising clinical candidate.

title: Interplay between SFTSV and host innate immunity: Viral evasion mechanisms, pathogenesis, and therapeutic perspectives

analysis.scope_and_question: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), caused by SFTSV, is an emerging tick-borne disease with substantial mortality in East Asia and increasing geographic reach.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: Here, we provide an updated conceptual framework that integrates classic host recognition via DNA and RNA sensors accompanied with the multifaceted immune evasion strategies orchestrated by the viral components.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: A central focus is that SFTSV utilizes host receptors for attachment and internalization while hijacking autophagy-related membranes to promote assembly and egress. Its NSs protein forms autophagic inclusion bodies that sequester and degrade innate immune factors, whereas NP and Gn interfere with RIG-I-MAVS and cGAS-STING signaling through autophagy-associated mechanisms.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Collectively, unraveling these intricate host-virus interactions will be pivotal for advancing targeted therapeutic strategies against SFTS.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: We also examine NS-driven inflammatory regulation and evidence that the microbiota shapes virus transmission and antiviral responses.

analysis.summary_en: This review discusses the mechanisms of SFTSV's interaction with host innate immunity, including viral evasion strategies and the role of the microbiota in virus transmission and antiviral responses. It highlights the importance of understanding these interactions for developing targeted therapeutic strategies.
